items.title: Small caps -11% off the high: the Sep/Oct drawdown now exceeds the Q1 Iran-War correction
items.idea: US small caps fell 3% last week and sit 11% below their high, back at a make-or-break support level with 200dma breadth hovering at a key line. The Sep/Oct correction is now bigger than the Q1 Iran-War one (via @evanmedeiros). Offsetting: Russell seasonality turns up after the weak stretch, especially in midterm years.
items.angle: Small caps are the rate-shock canary with the 10y above 5%. Seasonality vs. rates is the tension to trade.
items.tweetA: Small caps just fell harder on a 5% 10-year than they did during an actual war with Iran. That tells you which shock the Russell 2000 is more levered to. Seasonality says buy it; the 10-year says not yet. $IWM
items.tweetB: Everyone is arguing about AI multiples while IWM quietly did -11% off the high. If the 200dma breadth line breaks, the 'broadening' narrative loses its only live leg.

charts.desc: Small cap drawdown vs Q1 Iran-War correction; Russell seasonality chart

items.title: Smart money flips: big shorts in big tech, sizeable longs in small caps
items.idea: Per @i3_invest, positioning has shifted to large shorts in big tech and sizeable longs in small caps. Same edition: equal-weight S&P is +3% off the lows while cap-weighted is dragged by semis (SMH -10%, chips-heavy KOSPI -15%).
items.angle: Small caps -11% with smart money long them is either the best contrarian setup or a falling knife. Watch the 200dma line.
items.tweetA: Smart money is short mega-cap tech and long the asset class that just fell 11%. Either that's the cleanest contrarian trade of the quarter or it's a catching-knives club with good PR. The 200dma on IWM decides which.
items.tweetB: SMH -10% and KOSPI -15% in one week. The index shows a flat tape while the AI hardware complex gets repriced underneath. Equal weight +3% off lows isn't a rally, it's rotation.

charts.desc: Smart-money positioning shorts big tech / longs small caps; equal-weight vs cap-weight

items.title: Private equity stocks, tech CDS and margin debt all flashing at once
items.idea: PE stocks remain under pressure near key support, reflecting private credit worries, saturated flows and higher rates hurting the high-debt model. Tech CDS (plus telecom and media) is surging again as AI capex shifts the sector from cash flow to credit. Margin-debt acceleration rolled over from very high levels and is still in warning mode.
items.angle: Credit is where the AI capex bill shows up first. PE-stock support break is the trigger to watch.
items.tweetA: AI capex is turning the best credits in the market into credit stories. Tech CDS widening, PE stocks at support, margin debt rolling over. Three different markets telling you the cost of capital just became the variable.
items.tweetB: Hyperscalers used to fund capex out of free cash flow and now the CDS desk is pricing them. The first sign of an AI bust isn't a revenue miss, it's a spread. $KKR $BX

charts.desc: Tech CDS surge; PE stock index at support; margin debt acceleration indicator

items.title: AI-related stocks ~50% of the S&P; household equity allocation at an all-time high
items.idea: AI-linked names are around 50% of the index, echoing prior boom concentration (rails as the counter-precedent). Investor allocations look 'basically all-in', with US household equity allocation at a record. Sentiment is elevated but trending down; stance is 'pragmatically bullish'. Buyback blackouts lift the last week of October.
items.angle: Record allocation plus 50% concentration means the only marginal buyer left is the corporate buyback window.
items.tweetA: Households at record equity allocation, AI at ~50% of the index, and the one remaining bid is the corporate buyback window reopening in the last week of October. That's not a bull market, it's a calendar.
items.tweetB: Where's the marginal buyer when everyone is already all-in? The honest answer this month is companies themselves, and they are the ones now paying 5% for debt.

charts.desc: AI share of S&P ~50% vs historic concentration; household equity allocation ATH

items.title: 10y above 5.3% beat the S&P forward earnings yield for the first time since the dotcom bust
items.idea: When the 10-year pushed above 5.3% it exceeded the S&P 500 forward earnings yield for the first time since the end of the dotcom bust. Nasdaq is down ~5%, S&P barely off records. The author's framing: bonds don't need to be sexy, only competitive, which reopens the 60/40 debate.
items.angle: Equity risk premium negative again with AI leadership wobbling. This is the macro anchor for the week.
items.tweetA: 10-year at 5.3% over the S&P forward earnings yield. Bonds don't need to be sexy, they need to pay you not to own Meta. $TLT
items.tweetB: The 60/40 is back from the dead only because the 40 finally yields more than the 60's earnings. Ask who sells equities to buy duration when the S&P is still 1-2% off record highs.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Wall Street Week Ahead
items.title: Fed: October odds collapse to ~15% after Warsh refuses to date the next hike; December is the live domino
items.idea: CPI and PPI re-accelerated and PCE is still heading the wrong way, yet October hike odds fell to ~15% after Warsh in Bangkok wouldn't name a date. Policymakers face inflation saying tighten and credit saying sit still. The pivot variable is whether AI financing stress tightens conditions enough to do the Fed's work.
items.angle: Fed reaction function is now credit-conditional. Trade AI credit spreads as a Fed proxy.
items.tweetA: Inflation data says hike, credit says don't, and the market sided with credit in a day. If AI spreads are your Fed's hawk-suppressor, then the next hike is priced off CoreWeave bonds, not CPI.
items.tweetB: Core is accelerating across short annualized windows and October odds are 15%. Either the Fed is about to be wrong-footed by inflation, or credit stress is doing a hike's work for free. December tells us which.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Wall Street Week Ahead
items.title: Hyperscaler capex ~$1.2T next year; Meta earnings is the 'return on the next dollar' test
items.idea: Combined hyperscaler capex is expected near $1.2T next year, so each earnings call is partly a financing call. CoreWeave has shown what happens when the buildout meets the cost of money. SOX is down ~12% this month but still +57% YTD; Lam Research and TI are the breadth test, Meta the capex test.
items.angle: The bar moved from 'demand exists' to 'incremental ROIC clears a 5% risk-free rate'.
items.tweetA: $1.2T of hyperscaler capex against a 10-year at 5.3%. The question on Meta's call isn't growth, it's whether the next dollar of capex earns more than a Treasury. That bar didn't exist 18 months ago. $META
items.tweetB: SOX -12% this month and still +57% YTD. The semis aren't cheap, they're just less expensive than they were. $LRCX earnings is where we see if there's breadth under the hyperscaler story.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Wall Street Week Ahead
items.title: Market is an on/off switch: AI wobbles, healthcare and staples get a bid; Dems at ~80% for midterms
items.idea: AI-linked names under pressure while healthcare and consumer staples find a bid: when AI works it sucks oxygen out of the room, when it wobbles the rest of the market breathes. Prediction markets have a Democratic midterm sweep near 80%; the author notes Iran and trade don't wait for Congress, and that this part of the cycle is historically tougher.
items.angle: Defensive rotation plus gridlock odds; executive-driven risks (Iran, tariffs) stay unhedged by gridlock.
items.tweetA: Prediction markets say 80% Democratic sweep, which markets read as gridlock. But the two live risks, Iran and tariffs, are executive-branch trades. Gridlock hedges the wrong thing.
items.tweetB: Healthcare and staples are the AI trade's shock absorber right now. When the on/off switch flips back, the pain is in whatever got bought as a hedge this week.

items.title: Electricity Island: Russia warns NATO it would use nuclear weapons if Kaliningrad is cut off
items.idea: At the end of September Moscow sent NATO a note (seen by Reuters) saying it would use its full arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance tried to isolate Kaliningrad, including strikes on decision-making centers 'right from the outset'. Context: the Baltics synchronized to the Continental European grid on Feb 9 2025 with €1.23B of EU grants (75% of costs), leaving Kaliningrad's ~1M residents without direct power links. Doomberg points to energy flows as the likely tripwire.
items.angle: Energy infrastructure as nuclear tripwire. Baltic power, Nord-like gas and LNG logistics all become escalation vectors.
items.tweetA: Russia told NATO in writing it would go nuclear over Kaliningrad's isolation. The thing that got us here wasn't a tank, it was an electrical interconnector the EU paid €1.23B for. Grid policy is now arms control.
items.tweetB: Europe spent 15 years and €1.2B making the Baltics independent of Russian power. The cost: a 1M-person exclave whose power cutoff Moscow now calls a nuclear trigger. Nobody priced that in the TTF curve.

items.title: Week in numbers: QQQ -5.5%, SPY -2%, equal-weight +0.5% — 60% of S&P stocks closed up
items.idea: SPY -2%, QQQ -5.5%, IWM -3%, equal-weight +0.5%, Dow +0.6% on the week. 60% of S&P stocks closed up, 80% of 163 industry groups flat or up, 10 of 11 sectors outperformed the market, and tech was the only underperformer. The author: 'one of the best setups of the year', positioning was a minefield and is now being cleared.
items.angle: A 5.5% QQQ drop with 60% of stocks up is a pure concentration unwind, not a market selloff.
items.tweetA: QQQ -5.5%, and 60% of S&P stocks closed up. Ten of eleven sectors beat the index. That's not a selloff, that's one sector being repriced while the rest of the market learned to breathe.
items.tweetB: The headline index says panic. The breadth says rotation. Whoever is wrong, the P&L difference is whether you owned the Nasdaq or everything else last week.

items.title: Trend is down: SOXX -12% in a week, nine red days in a row, 5/21 cross down, NAAIM 74.5 vs 100
items.idea: Both SPX and Nasdaq broke their 50-dmas; SOXX fell 12% on heavy volume and is red nine straight days. VIX rose 30% but reads only 20; CPC 0.92 (below 1.0); Rydex Bull/Bear 0.05; NAAIM 74.53 from 100 in early September (60 in April). The author wants VIX near 30, a CPC spike and a July-lows revisit before buying; keep hedges while under the 50dma.
items.angle: No capitulation yet; a framework for what 'real fear' looks like with specific levels.
items.tweetA: SOXX down nine straight days and the VIX is still only 20. This is a 12% semi drawdown with 2019-style fear. I'd want VIX 30 and CPC well over 1 before calling a low.
items.tweetB: NAAIM went from 100 to 74.5 in six weeks. In April it hit 60 at the bottom. We're not even at the April fear level on a sector that just did -12% in a week.

items.title: Subscriber chat: rotating out of 'pure' AI names — out of CIFR and CRDO, trimming CRWV, exited TWST
items.idea: In the chat the author says they've moved away from 'pure' AI names (CIFR, CRDO exited; CRWV trimmed; TWST exited) and made three new bets. Mega-caps that do fine at higher rates aren't on sale yet. Advice: buy dips in the last 5-10 minutes of red sessions or large gaps down; cash is a must.
items.angle: A practitioner de-risking AI-beta specifically: Neocloud, photonic/connectivity, and bitcoin-miner AI hosting.
items.tweetA: Someone running a book is exiting CIFR and CRDO and trimming CRWV in one week. That's three different sub-sectors of the same trade: miners-turned-hosts, connectivity and neoclouds. All of them are levered to the cost of capital.
items.tweetB: When the practitioners start selling the 'pure' AI baskets before the hyperscaler prints, the beta is the thing they're short, not the thesis.

items.title: 'Old Habits': inflation prints beat by a wide margin yet markets went risk-off on AI
items.idea: All the week's inflation releases beat expectations by a substantial amount, yet markets were in risk-off mode on AI worries, with the VIX reacting late in the week after prolonged complacency. 'Old habits are hard to give up' in the bond market reaction. Also: his Australia theme, where monetary policy is beginning to bite, with trade ideas 'off to a great start'. Week ahead: NAHB, housing starts, S&P PMIs, UMich.
items.angle: Macro-prints beating and equities selling is a regime tell: equities are being priced off rates, not growth.
items.tweetA: Inflation beats, the market sells stocks and calls it an AI problem. It isn't. When good data is bad news, the discount rate is the whole story.
items.tweetB: Australia is where monetary policy is starting to bite. Everyone else is still debating whether they hike. If it bites there, ask who else is on the same lag.

items.title: Ledger hardware implant: ~$70-100M drained via LTE/eSIM chip in devices from authorized reseller CryptoBilis
items.idea: Genuine Ledger devices sold via CryptoBilis (SE Asia) shipped with an LTE chip and eSIM that intercepted seed phrases on their way to the screen, passing Ledger's genuine check. Losses are estimated at $70M-$100M over roughly four months, with panicked users then losing more to phishing and fake apps. Tarun Chitra: 'North Korea buying the liquor distributor'; Haseeb's advice: buy direct from the manufacturer.
items.angle: Hardware supply-chain attack on self-custody. Bullish regulated custody/ETF, bearish the narrative 'not your keys'.
items.tweetA: The attack on self-custody didn't break the cryptography. It added a $2 modem to the box. $100M gone because the weakest link was the reseller, not the secure element. $COIN custody just got a better pitch.
items.tweetB: Every crypto security model assumed the device in your hand was honest. A hidden eSIM that exfiltrates seed phrases is the hardware version of a dependency attack. The cost of trust just went up for anything that ships in a box.

items.title: Justin Drake: AI-accelerated math could break crypto cryptography 'in the worst case, in months, not years'
items.idea: Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake warned AI-accelerated math could break crypto's cryptography on a timeline of months in the worst case. ARK's Lorenzo Valente says quantum fears plus the Ledger hack are speeding up a trend ARK already saw: self-custody is slowly dying, and he would point a first-time bitcoin buyer to an ETF. Chris Perkins argues this may be the moment for intermediaries.
items.angle: Quantum/AI-crypto risk timeline compressing is a real shift in the BTC risk premium debate.
items.tweetA: An Ethereum Foundation researcher says AI could break the cryptography 'in months, not years' in the worst case, in the same week a hardware wallet was backdoored. Maybe the bear case for BTC isn't price, it's the keys. $BTC
items.tweetB: ARK says self-custody is dying and the fix is an ETF. So the argument for bitcoin ETFs just became: your own keys are the biggest risk in the asset. That's quietly the strongest bull case for $IBIT custodians.

items.title: ARK on crypto buybacks: 'the wrong way to allocate capital'; Strategy's STRC buyback loop and cash
items.idea: ARK's Lorenzo Valente calls the crypto buyback craze irrational, and notes Ethereum's L1 accrues so little value while Robinhood makes millions. Also linked: an explainer on Strategy's STRC buybacks covering cash, dilution and a $100 target, and whether the loop is running out of cash.
items.angle: Token buybacks vs. fee accrual is the valuation fight for L1s; STRC is the preferred-stock plumbing of the BTC treasury trade.
items.tweetA: ARK says buybacks are the wrong way to allocate capital in crypto. Robinhood makes millions off the same users whose ETH L1 accrues almost nothing. The value capture isn't in the protocol, it's in the front-end. $HOOD $ETH
items.tweetB: If a buyback requires issuing preferreds to fund it, it isn't a buyback, it's a financing loop. STRC at a $100 target is the most levered version of 'number go up' I can think of.

items.title: 'Drone hedgehog': three great powers can't beat a country with a large drone arsenal
items.idea: A drone hedgehog is a country with a large drone-fueled arsenal (aerial, ballistic, land, sea) able to fight a major power to a standstill or make attacks so costly they deter. The pairing: Russia vs Ukraine, US vs Iran, China vs Taiwan. A second piece flags 'minimum viable force' as the key restructuring question for militaries absorbing Ukraine's lessons.
items.angle: Cheap mass beats exquisite platforms, supporting drone/interceptor names and bearish legacy platform margins.
items.tweetA: Russia-Ukraine, US-Iran, China-Taiwan: same problem with different flags. The attacker has the exquisite platform; the defender has the 500-dollar drone factory. Defense budgets will tell you which one investors are underwriting.
items.tweetB: The hedgehog doesn't need to win. It just needs to make an invasion cost more than the invader's budget. That math is why Taiwan's drone program matters more than its F-16 order.

items.title: Ballistic missile defense: attackers produce missiles faster and cheaper than defenders produce interceptors
items.idea: A cited piece argues the West must leave its 'ballistic missile defense wonderland': where the attacker out-produces the defender on cost, either build a credible counterstrike capability and narrow BMD to short-term protection of critical assets, or bend the cost curve with mass-producible interceptors, as in Ukraine and other European programs, which remain unproven.
items.angle: Offense-defense cost imbalance is the investable thesis behind cheap interceptor programs.
items.tweetA: If it costs more to shoot down a missile than to build one, defense isn't deterrence, it's a subscription. The only way out is either counterstrike or interceptors at a fraction of unit cost. $LMT $RTX are priced for the former.
items.tweetB: The missile defense debate has become a unit-cost debate. Whoever solves the $50k interceptor wins a bigger contract than whoever builds the next $4M one.

items.title: Inference glut: 'we aren't overbuilding data centers, but we could'
items.idea: A quoted analysis says current projections don't show data-center overbuilding, but an inference glut isn't out of the question if estimates are off a bit; it tells readers what to watch for to exit the data-center trade or to buy up glut capacity. Elsewhere, a quoted argument that AI adoption doesn't cross the chasm until it goes from a '1980s computer you wire yourself' to an iPhone-style abstraction.
items.angle: A concrete exit signal: inference demand vs capacity. Tie to Meta/hyperscaler capex prints.
items.tweetA: No one's overbuilding data centers, until inference demand estimates miss by a little. Then the glut arrives and capacity gets cheap for whoever has cash. The AI capex trade isn't binary, it's a spread on utilization.
items.tweetB: Adoption is the missing variable. If AI is still a 1980s PC that needs wiring, then $1.2T of capex is pre-paying for an iPhone moment that hasn't happened.

items.title: Oil shock → fertilizer → farm costs → food CPI: the '1970s again' chain and the 4-5% alarm line
items.idea: Quoted chain: oil shock, fertilizer up, farm costs up, pass-through to consumers, headline inflation incl. food up. The Fed excludes food and energy, but that won't fly politically for long. 2021 peaked near 7%; a second wave of 4-5% would set off alarms. The curator's take: 'It's like the 1970s again and hard assets are a must.'
items.angle: Hard assets plus the supply-chain-of-inflation framing. Fertilizer is the transmission channel to watch.
items.tweetA: Oil shock to fertilizer to farm costs to grocery bills. The Fed excludes food and energy, voters don't. A 70s-style second wave would only need 4-5% to break the 'transitory' framing a second time.
items.tweetB: Core PCE is the Fed's lens and the grocery bill is the voter's. When they diverge for long enough, the political reaction function overrides the technocratic one. $DE $NTR

items.title: US captured 57% of 2025 global VC; the Bay Area took 60% of global AI funding
items.idea: Per a quoted piece on building outside the SF-NY axis: the US captured 57% of global venture funding in 2025 and the Bay Area alone took 60% of global AI funding. AI lowers the barriers to build and scale startups; the argument is that building fintech outside SF/NY means less competition and more product breadth. Also noted this week: 'SpaceX buys Cursor!'
items.angle: Geographic concentration of AI capital vs. the case for emerging-market founders.
items.tweetA: The Bay Area took 60% of global AI venture funding. That's not a cluster, that's a monoculture. And it means the cheap alpha in AI is wherever the capital isn't.
items.tweetB: SpaceX buying Cursor is the tell: the AI app layer is getting absorbed by whoever has the biggest balance sheet. Independent AI tool companies have a shrinking exit window.

items.title: Conspicuous leisure: the status signal shifts from Birkin bags to free time ('the time-filled economy')
items.idea: Quoted essay: the sheen of luxury possessions has tarnished; the new clout is conspicuous leisure (niche hobbies, exotic travel, creative output). Productivity tech lets us do more, 'time-back' tech lets us do less. If AI gives back discretionary hours, travel, dining, fitness, hobbies, learning and culture rise: a 'time-filled economy'.
items.angle: Second-order consumption shift if AI actually frees time; experiences over goods.
items.tweetA: If AI hands people back five hours a week, the winners aren't software companies, they're whatever people spend those hours on. The 'time-filled economy' is the demand side of the AI trade nobody models. $ABNB $CMG
items.tweetB: Luxury goods signaled money. The next signal is having time. That's a bear case for logo handbags and a bull case for anything that sells a Tuesday afternoon.

items.title: 'Lotto-ticket mentality': housing, student debt and tech monopolies push risk-taking; Situational Awareness blow-up as the annual wild event
items.idea: Quoted analysis: post-COVID 'nothing matters, everything is too expensive' leads to sports betting, 0DTE options and meme pumps; six-figure salaries no longer buy a home plus car. If income isn't rising faster than asset prices people feel behind; the ultra-rich and below-median both gamble. Result: immense demand for risk assets with much more volatile swings, with a 'Situational Awareness blow up' cited as this year's levered-position casualty.
items.angle: Structural demand for convexity: retail 0DTE and prediction markets as a wealth-gap symptom.
items.tweetA: The reward for being responsible got delayed by a decade, so people buy lottery tickets. That's not irrationality, it's a rational response to a housing market that makes savings pointless. It also means vol never goes away. $VIX
items.tweetB: Retail 0DTE, sports betting and prediction markets are all the same trade: cheap hope. The market structure keeps getting built for it. Watch who sells the other side.

items.title: 'Industrial legos': the end state of US manufacturing is specialist software-front firms, with AI deciding what's manufacturable
items.idea: Quoted piece: neither Shenzhen nor a fortress, but groups of narrow, productized specialists plugging into each other, with manufacturability checked by software at upload. Autodesk ships AI DFM reports in Fusion and startups put manufacturability inside CAD; whoever encodes real manufacturability decides what AI may design. Missing pieces: an asset class for pre-revenue machines, engineers, computable liability, interfaces that answer, cheap automation. The goal is having the option, not making everything domestically.
items.angle: Manufacturing as software: the DFM layer inside CAD is the choke point.
items.tweetA: Whoever encodes manufacturability decides what AI is allowed to design. That's a quiet chokepoint: not the model, not the chip, the DFM rules inside the CAD file. $ADSK
items.tweetB: America doesn't need to make everything. It needs the option to make anything. Right now there are whole component categories with no domestic supplier at any price or lead time. That's an asset class waiting for a name.

items.title: AI-psychosis hygiene: heavy AI-agent use detaches tech workers from reality
items.idea: A quoted piece describes Bay Area founders spending time with coding agents and growing disconnected from reality; one source warns 'It is increasingly important to have actively maintained cognitive security and cognitive hygiene.' One response: posting local restaurants and prioritizing in-person meetups. Separately noted: the Philippines has the youngest population among the top 40 economies and a US-military partnership that could make it an AI winner.
items.angle: Behavioral risk in the AI-builder class; also an EM demographic angle (Philippines).
items.tweetA: The people building the AI boom are warning each other about the AI boom's effect on their own heads. 'Cognitive hygiene' is the new burnout. That is the leading indicator for sentiment, not the VIX.
items.tweetB: Philippines: youngest population of the top 40 economies, plus a US security partnership. That's the same recipe that made Korea and Taiwan work, with an AI tailwind. $EPHE

items.title: Nu Holdings: first $1B+ net income quarter, serves a customer for <$1/month vs $4+ for traditional banks
items.idea: Nu earned over $1B of net income in a single quarter (Q2 2026) for the first time. It costs Nu under $1 a month to serve a customer against $4+ at traditional banks; 80-90% of new customers come from free referrals. LatAm banks earn ~$140B from everyday customers; Nu is expanding in Mexico and Colombia.
items.angle: A bank with fintech unit economics: cost-to-serve and zero CAC. LatAm penetration story.
items.tweetA: $1B quarterly profit from a bank with no branches. $1 a month to serve a customer against $4 for incumbents, and 80-90% of customers arrive for free. That's not a fintech multiple, that's a cost structure incumbents can't copy. $NU
items.tweetB: LatAm banks earn $140B from retail customers and Nu just proved you can take it with an app. Mexico and Colombia are the same movie with a different language.

items.title: October Best Buys: MercadoLibre 225M same/next-day shipments +38%; FICO losing its monopoly; Fortinet +137% YTD
items.idea: MercadoLibre shipped 225M same- and next-day packages last quarter, +38% YoY, via its own fulfillment network. Worst performer of the month: Fair Isaac (FICO), 'losing their monopoly'. Best: Fortinet, +137% YTD. Investor AB is a favorite but trades at a premium to NAV. The Fear & Greed index reads 'Fearful'; S&P was +1.8% in September.
items.angle: FICO monopoly erosion and MELI logistics moat are two single-name stories.
items.tweetA: 225M same-day shipments, +38%. MercadoLibre built the logistics in a region where the postal service doesn't work, and now competitors can't match the delivery speed. That's a moat made of trucks. $MELI
items.tweetB: FICO is getting punished for losing its scoring monopoly while Fortinet is +137% YTD. In a market panicking about AI, monopoly erosion is being priced faster than moat creation. $FICO $FTNT
